query: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, while other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems. Consequently, these precedents do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes. Within the defining constraint of a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, what governs superconducting behavior in such an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy, and why? State one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison against the starting material, predicted observations relative to the baseline, applicable boundary conditions, the earlier evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The superconducting behavior of the uncharacterized high‐entropy alloy is governed by the extent of atomic size mismatch–induced disorder that modulates electron–phonon coupling. Reducing the mismatch (and hence local lattice strain) enables stronger electron–phonon interactions, thereby enhancing the superconducting transition temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: An unmodified high‐entropy alloy synthesized as a single-phase solid solution containing at least five elements (each at ≥5 at.%) that naturally exhibits significant atomic size variations and associated lattice disorder.
generation.intervention: Substitute a fraction of the element with the largest atomic radius mismatch with another chemically similar element whose atomic radius is closer to the mean of the alloy. This maintains the minimum 5 at.% requirement for each element while reducing the overall atomic size spread.
generation.conditions: Synthesize both the baseline and modified alloys under identical conditions (same temperature profile, cooling rate, and processing route) to ensure a continuous solid solution. Superconducting properties are measured under zero magnetic field using standardized magnetization and resistivity protocols.
generation.structural_mediator: The local lattice disorder stemming from atomic size mismatch.
generation.mechanism: A large atomic size mismatch increases local strain and disorder, which can disrupt coherent electron pairing by scattering carriers and weakening electron–phonon coupling. By reducing this mismatch, local lattice strain decreases, thereby reinforcing electron–phonon coupling that promotes superconductivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline, the modified alloy is predicted to exhibit an increased superconducting transition temperature (Tc), reflecting enhanced electron–phonon coupling, although the exact magnitude of the increase is uncertain.
generation.baseline: The as-synthesized high‐entropy alloy with its inherent atomic size mismatch and corresponding lattice disorder.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to high‐entropy alloys prepared as single-phase solid solutions (with ≥5 elements at ≥5 at.% each) and measured under the specified controlled conditions; different synthesis routes or compositions may introduce additional effects.
generation.uncertainty: The exact numerical increase in Tc and the balance between disorder-induced pair-breaking and enhanced coupling are not precisely predictable due to the complex multi-element interactions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set being the baseline high‐entropy alloy and the other set modified by substituting a portion of the most size-mismatched element with a similarly behaving, size-compatible element. Ensure all other synthesis parameters are identical. Measure and compare their superconducting transition temperatures and electron–phonon coupling indicators (e.g., specific heat jump at Tc).
measurements: Superconducting transition temperature (Tc) via magnetization and resistivity measurements
Specific heat measurements near Tc to estimate electron–phonon coupling strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy does not show a statistically significant increase in Tc (or clear indications of enhanced electron–phonon coupling) compared to the baseline alloy, the hypothesis that reducing atomic size mismatch improves superconductivity would be falsified.
